title: Trump appointing an AI czar amid concerns over the rapidly developing tech
content:
President Donald Trump announced Saturday that he will appoint a czar to take point on artificial intelligence and will also create an AI task force.
The move comes after AI researchers warned that the technology could soon spiral out of human control, sparking concerns and calls for industry regulation.
Trump said in a social media post Saturday he would not let the “decimation” of AI happen.
“We will not in any way hinder or stifle the Growth of this incredible Industry. Rather, we will cherish it, help it, and watch over it, as it grows! However, we will also be looking for BAD, and we can do that, very easily, with our already existing Criminal and Civil Justice System. For this purpose, I am forming the AI Force, much like I did Space Force,” Trump said on Truth Social.
Trump added that “only High I.Q. individuals need apply” to the new AI czar role, to which he did not name an appointee in the post.
Trump has seemed unfazed by the warnings over the last two weeks, calling them a “hoax” and saying the priority should be for the U.S. to lead in AI development and beat China.
“Whoever wins AI wins,” Trump said multiple times over the last week.
In a flurry of social media posts, the president launched a full-throated defense of the technology, and he even called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang while Huang was onstage at an industry summit to talk about the issue.
The White House did not immediately provide more details on Trump’s new initiative.
While lawmakers on both sides of the aisle have attempted to advance legislation in the past few years, it has not gone anywhere. But members of Congress are once again discussing the issue amid renewed warnings.
During a closed-door briefing on the topic this week, Nobel laureate Geoffrey Hinton, known as the “godfather of AI,” warned lawmakers that time was running out to regulate the industry, telling them Congress has “maybe a year” to get the job done.
Trump previously had an AI and cryptocurrency czar, David Sacks, who stepped down earlier this year due to limits on his term as a special government employee. Sacks has since taken an advisory role in the administration and is expected to join Trump’s state dinner with Chinese leader Xi Jinping.
Democrats widely seen as 2028 presidential hopefuls have made moves to regulate AI at the state level.
California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed an executive order on Friday seeking to increase oversight of the industry and urged a task force to consider requiring the creation of a kill switch. Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro has called on the federal government to regulate AI, and Virginia Gov. Abigail Spanberger launched an AI task force and data center accountability plan aimed at addressing “growing concern and risks posed by the rapid development of artificial intelligence.”
Former President Barack Obama advised Democrats during an fundraiser last week to prioritize creating a plan on the issue and said he would make it a central issue if he were running in 2028.

report.summary: Trump says he will appoint an AI czar and create an 'AI Force' task force, prioritizing US AI growth over regulation amid safety warnings.
report.background: The announcement comes as AI capabilities advance rapidly, with researchers including Geoffrey Hinton warning Congress that regulation may have only about a year to act. Trump has dismissed such concerns as a 'hoax' and emphasized beating China in AI. The US has no comprehensive federal AI law; previous legislative efforts stalled. Trump earlier had an AI and crypto czar, David Sacks, who stepped down due to special-government-employee term limits and now advises the administration. Meanwhile, Democratic governors in California, Pennsylvania, and Virginia are pursuing state-level AI oversight, and former President Obama urged Democrats to make AI a central 2028 issue.
key_points: Trump announced on Truth Social that he will create an 'AI Force' and appoint an AI czar, though he did not name an appointee. He said 'only High I.Q. individuals need apply,' framing the effort as a way to oversee AI without slowing it.

Trump rejected calls for strict regulation, saying he will not 'hinder or stifle' the AI industry. He argued existing criminal and civil justice systems can handle 'BAD' actors, signaling a light-touch federal approach focused on growth and national competitiveness.

The move follows dire warnings from AI researchers that the technology could spiral out of human control. Hinton told lawmakers in a closed-door briefing that Congress has 'maybe a year' to regulate AI, intensifying pressure on policymakers.

Federal legislation has stalled for years, but states are acting. California's Gavin Newsom signed an executive order exploring a kill switch; Pennsylvania's Josh Shapiro and Virginia's Abigail Spanberger have pushed oversight and task forces, creating a fragmented regulatory landscape.

Trump has repeatedly said 'Whoever wins AI wins,' prioritizing US leadership over China. He even called Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang during an industry summit, underscoring his focus on AI as an economic and geopolitical race. The White House offered no further details on the czar's authority, budget, or timeline.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the announcement signals a federal emphasis on acceleration and competitiveness rather than prescriptive safety rules. Major labs and chipmakers may see continued political support, but the lack of federal law leaves a growing patchwork of state rules and potential compliance costs. Developers should watch for task-force recommendations, procurement standards, and any new reporting or security requirements. Regular users may get faster access to AI products, but with limited new federal safeguards; state-level proposals like kill switches could shape risk debates. The bigger question is whether an 'AI czar' can coordinate policy without statutory authority, especially as Congress remains divided and safety warnings intensify.
report.tools: To track and study these issues, follow the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, OECD AI Policy Observatory, Stanford AI Index, and AI Incident Database. For hands-on safety and evaluation, open-source tools include HELM, Inspect, Garak, and Hugging Face Evaluate. These help teams assess model risks and compare policy claims with technical evidence.
